title: find
description: GNU find — search for files in a directory hierarchy based on name, type, size, time, permissions, and more, then optionally act on the results. Part of GNU findutils, and installed by default on virtually every Linux system.

Getting Started.Getting Started:
`find` is part of GNU findutils, which also includes `locate` and
`xargs`. It ships preinstalled on essentially every Linux distribution.

## Current version

The latest stable release of GNU findutils is **4.11.0** (July 2026). The
core `find` expression syntax documented here has been stable across
findutils releases for a very long time — recent releases have focused on
portability, bug fixes, and small additions rather than syntax changes.

Worth knowing about: there is also a newer, independent **Rust
reimplementation**, [uutils/findutils](https://github.com/uutils/findutils)
(0.9.x as of mid-2026), aiming to be a drop-in replacement including
`locate`/`updatedb`. It is not what ships as `find` on Arch by default —
this guide covers GNU find.

## Check what you have

```bash
find --version
```

On Arch Linux, GNU findutils is part of the base system:

```bash
sudo pacman -S findutils
```

## Basic syntax

```bash
find [PATH...] [EXPRESSION]
```

- `PATH...` is where to start searching (defaults to `.`, the current
  directory, if omitted).
- `EXPRESSION` is a combination of tests, actions, and operators. If no
  expression is given, `-print` is assumed.

## Your first search

```bash
find . -name "*.dart"
```

Searches recursively from the current directory for files/directories
whose name matches the glob `*.dart`.

```bash
find /var/log -name "*.log"
find lib/ -type f -name "*.g.dart"
```

See [Core Concepts](/find/core-concepts/) for how `find`'s expression
grammar (tests, actions, operators) fits together, and
[Common Options](/find/common-options/) for the flag reference.
Getting Started.Core Concepts:
## The expression grammar

A `find` command line is built from three kinds of expression parts,
which is the single most important thing to understand about how `find`
differs from most other Unix tools:

1. **Tests** — evaluate to true/false for each file (`-name`, `-type`,
   `-size`, `-mtime`, `-newer`, etc.).
2. **Actions** — do something with matching files (`-print`, `-delete`,
   `-exec`, `-fprint`, etc.).
3. **Operators** — combine tests logically (`-a`/implicit AND, `-o`/OR,
   `!`/NOT, `( )` grouping).

```bash
find . -type f -name "*.dart" -a -newer pubspec.yaml
```

reads as: type is file, AND name matches `*.dart`, AND is newer than
`pubspec.yaml`. `-a` is implicit between adjacent tests — you rarely need
to write it explicitly.

```bash
find . \( -name "*.tmp" -o -name "*.bak" \) -delete
```

Parentheses need to be escaped (`\(`, `\)`) or quoted, since the shell
would otherwise interpret them as subshell syntax.

## Exit status

`0` if `find` ran with no errors (regardless of whether anything matched),
non-zero if an error occurred (e.g. permission denied on a directory it
couldn't read — though it continues searching what it can).

Unlike `grep`/`ripgrep`/`fd`, `find`'s exit code does **not** tell you
whether anything matched — that's a common gotcha. To check for a match in
a script, capture and inspect the output instead:

```bash
if [ -n "$(find . -name '*.dart' -print -quit)" ]; then
  echo "found at least one"
fi
```

## No ignore-file awareness

Plain GNU `find` has no concept of `.gitignore` — it walks the entire
filesystem tree as-is. If you want gitignore-aware recursive search, reach
for `fd` or `ripgrep --files` instead; see the companion docs for those
tools.

## Symlink handling

By default `find` does not follow symlinks when traversing (`-P`,
the default). `-L` makes it follow them; `-H` follows symlinks given
directly on the command line but not those discovered during traversal.

```bash
find -L /etc -name "*.conf"     # follow all symlinks
```

See [Tests & Filters](/find/tests-and-filters/) for the full test
reference and [Actions & -exec](/find/actions-and-exec/) for acting on
results.

Guides.Tests & Filters:
## Name matching

```bash
find . -name "*.dart"          # case-sensitive glob match on basename
find . -iname "*.DART"          # case-insensitive
find . -path "*/lib/*.dart"     # match against the whole path
find . -regex ".*\.dart$"       # full path, regex (see -regextype below)
```

`-name`/`-iname` match against the basename only; `-path`/`-ipath` and
`-regex`/`-iregex` match against the whole path.

## Regex dialects

```bash
find . -regextype posix-extended -regex ".*\.(dart|yaml)$"
```

`-regextype` is positional — it only affects `-regex`/`-iregex` tests that
appear *after* it on the command line. GNU findutils defaults to Emacs
regex syntax unless `-regextype` is given; common values include
`emacs` (default), `posix-basic`, `posix-extended`, `posix-egrep`.

## Type filters

```bash
find . -type f      # regular files
find . -type d      # directories
find . -type l      # symbolic links
find . -type f,l    # multiple types at once (comma-separated, GNU extension)
```

## Size filters

```bash
find . -size +10M     # larger than 10 MB
find . -size -1k       # smaller than 1 KB
find . -size 0         # exactly empty
find . -empty          # empty files or directories (shorthand)
```

## Time filters

| Test | Unit | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `-mtime N` | days | Modified N*24h ago (rounded). |
| `-mmin N` | minutes | Modified N minutes ago. |
| `-atime` / `-amin` | | Same, for access time. |
| `-ctime` / `-cmin` | | Same, for inode change time. |
| `-newer FILE` | | Modified more recently than FILE. |

```bash
find . -mtime -7            # modified within the last 7 days
find . -mmin -60             # modified within the last 60 minutes
find . -newer pubspec.yaml   # newer than a reference file
```

`+N` means "more than N", `-N` means "less than N", bare `N` means
"exactly N" (for time tests, within the relevant rounding unit).

## Depth control

```bash
find . -maxdepth 1 -type f      # only the current directory, no recursion
find . -mindepth 2 -type f      # skip the first level
```

## Permission and ownership

```bash
find . -perm 644              # exact permission match
find . -perm -u+x              # at least this bit set (executable by owner)
find . -user psdk              # owned by user "psdk"
find . -group wheel            # owned by group "wheel"
```

## Combining with logical operators

```bash
find . -type f \( -name "*.dart" -o -name "*.yaml" \) -not -path "*/build/*"
```

See [Actions & -exec](/find/actions-and-exec/) for what to do with the
matches.
Guides.Actions & -exec:
## -print, -print0

```bash
find . -name "*.dart"          # -print is implied when no action is given
find . -name "*.dart" -print0 | xargs -0 wc -l
```

`-print0` NUL-separates results, safe for piping into `xargs -0` when
filenames may contain spaces or newlines — always prefer this over plain
`-print` when piping to `xargs`.

## -exec: run a command per result

```bash
find . -name "*.dart" -exec dart format {} \;
```

`{}` is replaced with the current file path; the expression must end in
`\;` (escaped semicolon) or `+`.

## -exec ... + : run a command once with all results (like xargs)

```bash
find . -name "*.dart" -exec dart format {} +
```

Using `+` instead of `\;` batches as many matches as possible into fewer
invocations — much faster than the semicolon form for commands that
accept multiple file arguments, and avoids a separate `xargs` step.

## -delete

```bash
find . -name "*.tmp" -delete
```

Deletes matches directly. **Always dry-run first** by replacing `-delete`
with `-print` to see what would be removed:

```bash
find . -name "*.tmp" -print      # check first
find . -name "*.tmp" -delete     # then delete
```

`-delete` implies `-depth` (process directory contents before the
directory itself) automatically, since you can't otherwise safely delete
a non-empty directory.

## -ok: like -exec but asks for confirmation

```bash
find . -name "*.bak" -ok rm {} \;
```

Prompts `y/n` for each match before running the command — useful for
destructive operations you want to review interactively.

## Combining find with xargs directly

```bash
find . -name "*.dart" -print0 | xargs -0 -I{} dart format {}
```

Generally, prefer `-exec ... +` over piping to `xargs` when possible —
it's one less process and handles filenames with spaces correctly without
needing `-print0`/`-0`. Use the `xargs` pipeline when you need `xargs`-only
features like `-P` (parallel execution).

```bash
find . -name "*.dart" -print0 | xargs -0 -P4 -I{} dart format {}
```

See [Recipes](/find/recipes/) for these assembled into full workflows.
Guides.Recipes:
## Find and format every Dart file

```bash
find . -name "*.dart" -exec dart format {} +
```

## Delete all build artifacts (dry run first)

```bash
find . -type d \( -name build -o -name .dart_tool \) -print   # preview
find . -type d \( -name build -o -name .dart_tool \) -exec rm -rf {} +
```

## Find files larger than 50 MB anywhere under a path

```bash
find /home -size +50M -type f
```

## Find and archive files modified in the last day

```bash
find . -mtime -1 -type f -print0 | tar --null -czf recent.tar.gz --files-from=-
```

## Find empty directories and remove them

```bash
find . -type d -empty -delete
```

## Search excluding a directory (e.g. .git, node_modules)

```bash
find . -path "./.git" -prune -o -type f -name "*.dart" -print
```

`-prune` stops `find` from descending into a matched directory entirely —
much more efficient than filtering it out after the fact with `-not -path`,
especially on large trees like `node_modules`.

## Find files owned by a specific user

```bash
find /srv -user psdk -type f
```

## Find and count lines in matching files

```bash
find . -name "*.dart" -exec wc -l {} + | tail -1
```

## Use find purely for its side effect in a script

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
find . -maxdepth 1 -name "pubspec.yaml" -exec echo "Dart project detected" \;
```

## Combine with locate for fast name-only lookups on a whole system

```bash
sudo updatedb          # refresh the locate database (often runs via cron)
locate pubspec.yaml     # much faster than find / -name for whole-system search
```

`locate` trades freshness (its database updates periodically, not live)
for speed, since it doesn't walk the filesystem at query time.

Project.FAQ:
### Why doesn't `find`'s exit code tell me if anything matched?

By design — `find`'s exit status reflects whether it ran without errors,
not whether it found matches. To check for a match in scripts, inspect the
captured output, or use `-print -quit` to stop at the first hit.

### Why do I need to escape parentheses and semicolons?

`(`, `)`, and `;` are shell metacharacters. `find` needs them literally, so
they must be escaped (`\(`, `\)`, `\;`) or quoted (`'('`, `')'`, `';'`) to
reach `find` unmodified instead of being interpreted by the shell first.

### What's the difference between `-exec cmd {} \;` and `-exec cmd {} +`?

The `\;` form runs the command once per matching file (like a loop). The
`+` form batches as many matches as will fit into as few invocations as
possible — usually much faster, and equivalent to what `xargs` does, but
without needing a separate pipeline stage.

### How do I exclude a directory like `node_modules` efficiently?

Use `-prune`, not `-not -path`. `-prune` stops `find` from descending into
the directory at all; `-not -path` still walks the whole tree and just
hides matching results afterward, which is much slower on large excluded
trees:

```bash
find . -path "./node_modules" -prune -o -print
```

### Does `find` respect `.gitignore`?

No, never — that's not a concept GNU find has any awareness of. If you
want that behavior, use `fd` or `ripgrep --files` instead.

### `find` vs `locate` — which should I use?

`find` walks the filesystem live, so results are always current but
searching a large tree is slower. `locate` queries a prebuilt database
(refreshed periodically via `updatedb`, often by cron), so it's much
faster but can miss very recently created/deleted files until the next
database refresh.

### Is there a modern alternative?

Yes — `fd` (see the companion fd docs) offers gitignore-aware defaults,
parallel traversal, and friendlier syntax for the common cases, while
`find` remains the more complete, POSIX-adjacent tool with the deepest
expression language and the widest guaranteed availability.

### Where do I report bugs or read the changelog?

GNU findutils is maintained as part of the GNU project; see
[gnu.org/software/findutils](https://www.gnu.org/software/findutils/) and
the project's Savannah page for source, mailing lists, and release
history.

CLI Reference.find:
## Synopsis

```
find [-H] [-L] [-P] [-D debugopts] [-Olevel] [PATH...] [EXPRESSION]
```

A consolidated reference of GNU find's tests, actions, and options; see [Tests & Filters](/find/tests-and-filters/) and [Actions & -exec](/find/actions-and-exec/) for explanation and examples.

## Global options (before the path/expression)

| Option | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `-P` | Never follow symlinks (default) |
| `-L` | Follow all symlinks during traversal |
| `-H` | Follow symlinks named directly on the command line only |
| `-D debugopts` | Print diagnostic info (`tree`, `exec`, `opt`, etc.) — for debugging find itself |
| `-Olevel` | Query optimization level (`0`-`3`); rarely needs manual tuning |
| `--help` / `--version` | Show usage / version and exit |

## Options affecting traversal (go right after the path)

| Option | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `-maxdepth N` | Don't descend more than N levels |
| `-mindepth N` | Don't apply tests/actions until N levels deep |
| `-depth` | Process a directory's contents before the directory itself (implied by `-delete`) |
| `-mount`, `-xdev` | Don't cross filesystem/mount-point boundaries |
| `-noleaf` | Don't assume Unix hard-link counts to optimize directory checks (needed on some non-Unix filesystems) |
| `-regextype TYPE` | Regex dialect for later `-regex`/`-iregex` tests: `emacs` (default), `posix-basic`, `posix-extended`, `posix-egrep`, `sed`, `awk` |
| `-daystart` | Measure `-amin`/`-atime` etc. from the start of today, not 24h ago |
| `-warn` / `-nowarn` | Enable/disable find's own usage warnings |

## Name and path tests

| Test | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `-name PATTERN` | Basename matches glob (case-sensitive) |
| `-iname PATTERN` | Case-insensitive `-name` |
| `-path PATTERN` | Full path matches glob |
| `-ipath PATTERN` | Case-insensitive `-path` |
| `-wholename PATTERN` | GNU synonym for `-path` |
| `-regex PATTERN` | Full path matches regex (dialect set by `-regextype`) |
| `-iregex PATTERN` | Case-insensitive `-regex` |
| `-lname PATTERN` | Symlink target matches glob |
| `-ilname PATTERN` | Case-insensitive `-lname` |

## Type, size, and structure tests

| Test | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `-type C` | `f` file, `d` dir, `l` symlink, `b`/`c` block/char device, `p` pipe, `s` socket; comma-separated list for multiple |
| `-xtype C` | Like `-type` but dereferences symlinks first |
| `-size N[cwbkMG]` | Size in bytes(`c`)/words(`w`)/512B-blocks(`b`, default)/KB/MB/GB; `+`/`-` prefix for greater/less |
| `-empty` | Empty regular file or directory |
| `-links N` | Has N hard links |
| `-inum N` | Has inode number N |
| `-samefile FILE` | Refers to the same inode as FILE |

## Time tests

| Test | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `-mtime N` / `-mmin N` | Modified N days / minutes ago |
| `-atime N` / `-amin N` | Accessed N days / minutes ago |
| `-ctime N` / `-cmin N` | Inode changed N days / minutes ago |
| `-newer FILE` | Modified more recently than FILE |
| `-newerXY FILE` | Compare time field `X` of the found file to time field `Y` of FILE (`X`/`Y` from `a`,`c`,`m`,`B`(birth),`t`) |
| `-anewer FILE` / `-cnewer FILE` | Access/change time newer than FILE's respective field |

## Ownership and permissions

| Test | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `-user NAME` | Owned by user NAME (or UID) |
| `-group NAME` | Owned by group NAME (or GID) |
| `-uid N` / `-gid N` | Owned by numeric UID/GID |
| `-nouser` / `-nogroup` | No user/group in `/etc/passwd`/`/etc/group` owns this file |
| `-perm MODE` | Exact permission match |
| `-perm -MODE` | All of these bits are set |
| `-perm /MODE` | Any of these bits are set |
| `-readable` / `-writable` / `-executable` | Current user has that access right |

## Filesystem and misc tests

| Test | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `-fstype TYPE` | On a filesystem of the given type (e.g. `ext4`, `tmpfs`) |
| `-context PATTERN` | SELinux security context matches (glob) |
| `-used N` | Accessed N days after its inode was last changed |
| `-true` / `-false` | Always true / always false (mostly for testing expressions) |

## Actions

| Action | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `-print` | Print the path, newline-terminated (default if no action given) |
| `-print0` | Print the path, NUL-terminated |
| `-printf FORMAT` | Print using a `printf`-style format with find's own directives (`%p` path, `%s` size, `%m` perms, ...) |
| `-fprint FILE` / `-fprint0 FILE` / `-fprintf FILE FORMAT` | Same as above but write to `FILE` instead of stdout |
| `-ls` | Print `ls -dils`-style detail |
| `-fls FILE` | Same, written to `FILE` |
| `-delete` | Delete the matched file/directory (implies `-depth`) |
| `-exec CMD ARGS ; ` | Run `CMD` once per match, `{}` substituted, terminated with `\;` |
| `-exec CMD ARGS {} +` | Run `CMD` once with as many matches batched in as possible |
| `-execdir CMD ARGS ;`/`+` | Like `-exec` but runs with CWD set to the match's containing directory (safer against races) |
| `-ok CMD ARGS ;` | Like `-exec ... ;` but prompts for confirmation first |
| `-okdir CMD ARGS ;` | Like `-execdir` but prompts for confirmation first |
| `-prune` | Don't descend into this directory (only meaningful combined with `-o`) |
| `-quit` | Stop `find` immediately |

## Operators (highest to lowest precedence)

| Operator | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `( EXPR )` | Grouping (parentheses must be escaped/quoted for the shell) |
| `! EXPR`, `-not EXPR` | Negation |
| `EXPR1 EXPR2`, `EXPR1 -a EXPR2`, `EXPR1 -and EXPR2` | Logical AND (implicit between adjacent tests) |
| `EXPR1 -o EXPR2`, `EXPR1 -or EXPR2` | Logical OR |
| `EXPR1 , EXPR2` | List: evaluate both, result is EXPR2's (rare; for running two independent actions per file) |

Full manual: `man find`, or the [GNU findutils manual](https://www.gnu.org/software/findutils/manual/html_mono/find.html).

Learn by Examples.Auditing And Cleaning A Shared Server Di:
A shared `/srv/uploads` directory on a Linux box has grown messy over the years — stale files, wrong ownership from a departed user account, a few oversized uploads eating disk space. This walkthrough uses `find` end to end to audit and clean it safely.

## 1. Get a baseline

```bash
find /srv/uploads -type f | wc -l
```

Plain `-type f` piped to `wc -l` gives a file count before anything changes.

## 2. Find files owned by an account that no longer exists

```bash
find /srv/uploads -nouser -o -nogroup
```

`-nouser`/`-nogroup` catch files whose owning UID/GID isn't in `/etc/passwd`/`/etc/group` at all — a common sign of a deleted user account, and worth reassigning to a current owner rather than leaving orphaned.

## 3. Preview reassigning ownership (dry run via -print, then act)

```bash
find /srv/uploads -nouser -print
sudo find /srv/uploads -nouser -exec chown srv-uploads {} +
```

`-exec ... +` batches every match into as few `chown` invocations as possible instead of one process per file.

## 4. Find oversized uploads

```bash
find /srv/uploads -type f -size +100M -printf "%s\t%p\n" | sort -rn
```

`-printf` with a custom format prints size (`%s`) and path (`%p`) separated by a tab; piping through `sort -rn` ranks the biggest offenders first — more informative than plain `-print` when the point is prioritizing what to deal with first.

## 5. Find genuinely stale files, excluding an active subdirectory

```bash
find /srv/uploads -path /srv/uploads/active -prune -o -type f -mtime +365 -print
```

`-prune` on the `active` subtree stops `find` from even descending into it, which is both faster and semantically correct — those are current, in-use files that happen to be old, not candidates for cleanup.

## 6. Cross-check against a list of files known to matter

```bash
find /srv/uploads -type f -mtime +365 -print0 | \
  xargs -0 -I{} sh -c 'grep -qxF "{}" keep-list.txt || echo "{}"'
```

For each stale-by-time candidate, checks whether it's in a hand-maintained `keep-list.txt` of files that must never be auto-deleted, printing only the ones that are safe to remove — this kind of care matters more than any single flag once real deletion is on the table.

## 7. Archive before deleting

```bash
find /srv/uploads -type f -mtime +365 -not -newer keep-list.txt -print0 | \
  tar --null -czf stale-uploads-$(date +%F).tar.gz --files-from=-
```

Archiving the exact same file set that's about to be deleted means the operation is reversible if something was missed.

## 8. Delete, finally, with -depth semantics handled automatically

```bash
find /srv/uploads -type f -mtime +365 -delete
find /srv/uploads -type d -empty -delete
```

Run in two passes: files first, then any directories left empty as a result — `-delete` implies `-depth` so it never tries to remove a directory before its contents.

## 9. Confirm the result

```bash
find /srv/uploads -type f | wc -l
du -sh /srv/uploads
```

## What this walkthrough covered

`-nouser`/`-nogroup`, `-exec ... +`, `-printf` custom formatting, `-prune` for excluding an active subtree, `-print0` piped into `xargs -0` for cross-referencing against another file, combining with `tar --files-from=-` for a safety archive, and `-delete` in a files-then-directories order — the realistic, safety-conscious shape of a real cleanup task rather than a single one-liner.
